cards.title: First time renters
cards.prompt: Design a product that helps people renting their first apartment in a big city.
brief_lines: Users: first time renters in a big city
Goal: help them rent their first place
facts_if_asked: You're a new team with no existing product.
The company's goal is to build trust with young adults who'll later buy other financial products.
follow_ups: Who exactly is a first time renter?
Why that group first?
How would you know the problem is real?
What's the smallest version you'd build?
What would make you stop?
cards.twist: A year later the product works in one city. What does version two look like, and what would you not build?
strong_answer_covers: Segments such as students, relocating workers, people moving out of family homes; picks one with a reason
Real pains: deposits, scams, unknown neighbourhoods, credit history, paperwork
Prioritises pains by severity and frequency
A first version such as verified listings plus deposit protection, scoped to weeks
Success metric such as leases signed through the product, scam reports as a guardrail
Trust as the core risk, with a mitigation

cards.title: Library app for teens
cards.prompt: Improve a public library's app for teenagers.
brief_lines: Goal: more teens using the library
facts_if_asked: The current app is a catalogue search with accounts; teens rarely use it.
The library has study rooms, events, a makerspace and free wifi.
A small team: two engineers and a designer for six months.
follow_ups: Why don't teens use the app today?
Which teens?
What would they open it for, once a week?
How would you measure success?
cards.twist: The library's budget is cut and you can keep only one feature. Which, and why?
strong_answer_covers: Understands why teens don't use it, beyond the catalogue
Ideas beyond books: study room booking, events, social reading, homework help
Picks one with reach and effort reasoning
Respects privacy and safety for minors
Metric such as weekly active teen members, with a guardrail

cards.title: Museum smart glasses
cards.prompt: Design an experience for museum visitors wearing smart glasses.
brief_lines: Device: smart glasses with a camera, display and audio
facts_if_asked: Glasses can see what the wearer looks at and show short text or play audio.
The museum is large and has visitors from many countries.
The museum wants more repeat visits and more members.
follow_ups: Which visitors, exactly?
What's different about using glasses versus a phone here?
What about other visitors being filmed?
What would you test first?
cards.twist: Visitors love it, but the museum says crowds now stand still for too long in popular rooms. What do you change?
strong_answer_covers: Segments: tourists, families, people with visual or hearing needs, regulars
Context of use: hands free, short attention, walking
Privacy of other visitors
First version such as look to learn labels in the visitor's language
Metric tied to the museum's goal, such as membership sign ups, with crowding or dwell time as a guardrail
Designs for glasses, not a phone app moved onto them

cards.title: AI in a grocery app
cards.prompt: Build a feature for a grocery delivery app that uses AI.
brief_lines: Ask: a feature that uses AI
facts_if_asked: The app has five million monthly users, most ordering weekly.
Average basket is about seventy dollars.
The company wants larger baskets and more weekly orders.
The app knows past orders, but not what's in the fridge.
follow_ups: What user problem does this solve?
Why does it need AI?
What happens when the AI gets it wrong?
How would users come to trust it?
cards.twist: Your feature swaps an out of stock item and a customer gets the wrong thing for an allergy. What do you change?
strong_answer_covers: Starts from a user problem such as weekly meal planning, budget or substitutions, not from AI
Picks a segment with a reason
A first version with a clear role for AI
Risks: wrong substitutions, allergies, trust, with guardrails
Metric such as weekly order rate or basket size, with complaint or refund rate as a guardrail

cards.title: Less food waste for small restaurants
cards.prompt: Design a product that helps small, independent restaurants waste less food.
facts_if_asked: A typical restaurant throws away five to ten percent of what it buys.
Owners are busy and rarely at a desk.
Many use a basic point of sale system already.
follow_ups: Who in the restaurant would use it?
Where does the waste actually happen?
Why haven't they fixed this already?
How would you charge for it?
cards.twist: A large chain wants to buy it. What would have to change, and would you do it?
strong_answer_covers: Knows who the user is: owner, chef, or kitchen manager
Finds where waste happens: over ordering, prep, spoilage, unsold dishes
Picks one with a reason
A low effort first version that fits a busy kitchen
Metric such as waste as a share of purchases, with time spent per day as a guardrail
Does not assume busy owners will enter data by hand every day
